title: What May You Do

post.author: u/tollemache_stagedoor_faustina
post.title: I keep the stage door at a theatre. At 02:00 last night our ticket printer deleted every costume booking for the season. The database says it was allowed to.

blocks.text: I'm Faustina, stage-door keeper at the Tollemache Theatre. My whole job is knowing who may go where backstage. A dresser may go to wardrobe, never to the cash office. I check every pass, every night.

The theatre runs on three programs, which Afonso, who writes our software, calls systems. The box office sells tickets. Costume hire rents our old costumes to schools and touring companies. Payroll books staff shifts.
All three keep their bookings in one database, an organised store of records. The bookings sit in one shared list, called a table, one booking per line.
A label on each line, its kind, says whose it is: ticket, custom, costume or shift.

A program signs in to the database the way I sign in to my email, with a name and a password. A sign-in used by a program, not a person, is called a service account. In June Afonso set up one service account, theatre_all, for all three systems, with full rights: it may read, change or delete any booking. "To save time," he says.

Our ticket printer also makes custom tickets, with a guest's name on, for gifts. Unused drafts pile up. So since 1 September a small program, a script, has run at 02:00 every night under theatre_all to delete them. Afonso calls it the clean-up job.

Its instruction to the database ends in a filter, the part that picks which lines to delete. On Wednesday afternoon Afonso tidied the script and retyped that line. Here is the filter as it should read, and as it ran. Lines starting with two dashes are his notes; each other line says: delete every booking of this kind.

-- meant: delete the printer's custom ticket drafts
DELETE FROM bookings WHERE kind = 'custom'
-- ran: retyped from memory, and the filter named the costume hires
DELETE FROM bookings WHERE kind = 'costume'
It had run clean for 44 nights. At 02:00 on Thursday it did exactly what it was told. Nothing alerted anyone: the script only writes 'done' in a file nobody reads at night.

At 06:00 the costume system prints me the day's collections, so I know which couriers to let in. This morning it printed one line: no collections today. At 07:15 a school's courier came for 30 sailor suits, with the booking email in her hand. I rang Afonso.

The database keeps an audit log, its own diary of every change. Each line shows the date, the time, the action, the kind, how many rows (lines) it touched, and whether the database allowed it. It doesn't note which account asked.

14 Oct 02:00:03  DELETE  kind=custom   rows 37     allowed
15 Oct 02:00:04  DELETE  kind=costume  rows 1,860  allowed

Nothing else in the building runs at 02:00. So that is the ticket printer, deleting all 1,860 costume hires for the season: records it never needed and should never have been able to see. Every line is valid. The account was allowed.

blocks.label: who_can_reach_what.png

diagram.aria: How the theatre was set up last night. Four programs on the left, the box office, costume hire, payroll and the printer's clean-up job, all sign in as one service account, theatre_all, in the middle. theatre_all has full rights over all four kinds of booking on the right: 38,400 tickets, 41 custom drafts, 1,860 costume hires, deleted at 02:00:04, and 2,940 payroll shifts.

blocks.caption: Redrawn by Afonso from the database's settings, as they stood last night. Every system, and the printer's clean-up job, signs in as theatre_all, and theatre_all may read, change or delete all four kinds: 43,241 bookings in all. At 02:00:04 the job's filter named the costume hires, and nothing stood in its way. The 41 custom drafts it was meant for are still there.

blocks.text: Afonso put back the costume bookings from Sunday night's backup, the weekly safety copy of the database: 1,796 came back. Bronislava, at the costume desk, is rebuilding the 64 made since from emails. Payroll's 2,940 shifts sit under the same account. What should we change before the job runs again tonight?

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Two questions meet at every door, Faustina. Who are you? That's authentication, proving who someone is: your pass check, or the password theatre_all gave at 02:00. What may you do? That's authorization, deciding what someone already proven may do. The database got the first one right. Look at the second. Which kinds of booking does the printer's job ever need? Which could it touch at 02:00? If payroll had made the same slip, what would that log line have said? And how old is your newest copy?

replies.author: u/tollemache_stagedoor_faustina
replies.text: Afonso says the job only ever needs the custom drafts: 41 last night. At 02:00 it could touch all 43,241 bookings, the same as every system. Payroll's slip would have left the very same kind of line: a time, a kind, a count, allowed. Our newest copy was Sunday's.

comments.author: u/one_login_quirino
comments.text: One account is simpler to manage, and simple is secure. Split it into three and you have three passwords to keep safe and three lists of rights to get wrong. The account didn't fail; a typo did. Have a second person read every clean-up script's filter before it runs. Two pairs of eyes would have seen 'costume' in a second.

comments.author: u/restore_it_wiremu
comments.text: Slips happen whatever you build. Your weekly backup lost you 64 bookings. Take one every night instead and practise putting it back, and a wiped season costs you a few hours before Bronislava's desk opens at 09:00.

reply.prompt: The clean-up job runs again tonight at 02:00, and most of the season's bookings are back. What should Afonso change first? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Have a second person check every clean-up script's filter before it is allowed to run.
options.verdict: Catches this slip, not the reach
options.part2: Afonso now shows Bronislava every clean-up script's filter before it runs, and she reads it aloud. We replayed last night in the sim with the slip and the check: she spots 'costume', it goes back to 'custom', and the job deletes the 41 drafts and nothing else. Quirino was right about last night. But the access grid didn't change. The job still signs in as theatre_all, which may delete all 43,241 bookings, payroll's 2,940 shifts among them. The check catches the slips a reader spots, on the scripts someone remembers to show her. A slip she misses still meets no locked door, and the log still can't say which system asked.
options.senior: A second reader is a good habit and a weak control. It depends on a person noticing, every time, on every change, and it does nothing about what the account may reach. Protection that survives a missed mistake lives in the database's own rules: the job's account should be unable to touch costume hires at all. Keep the reading; don't let it stand in for narrow rights.

options.text: Take nightly backups of the costume bookings, so any wiped season can be put back by 9am.
options.part2: Afonso set the backup to run every night at 23:00. We replayed last night in the sim with the slip and a nightly copy: the job still deleted all 1,860 costume hires, and the 23:00 copy gave back 1,857. The 3 booked online after 23:00 were lost and had to come from emails. That is far better than Sunday's copy, which gave back 1,796 and lost 64, and Wiremu is right that a theatre needs it. But the delete happened just the same, and the grid shows the job can still reach payroll's 2,940 shifts.
options.senior: Backups decide how much you lose after a mistake; access rules decide whether the mistake can land at all. You need both, and they answer different questions. A nightly copy shrinks the gap to hours, never to zero: whatever changed after the last copy is gone, and putting a copy back usually takes care, because other bookings may have changed since. Keep the backup as the second line, behind narrow rights.

options.text: Add the account's name to every delete in the audit log, so a slip is traced in minutes.
options.verdict: It names everyone, so no one
options.part2: Afonso turned on account names in the audit log. We replayed last night in the sim with the slip: 02:00:04, DELETE, kind=costume, rows 1,860, allowed, and now a name, theatre_all. Box office, costume hire and payroll would all leave that same name, because they all sign in as it. The log names an account that is everybody, so it points at no one. And it still writes its line after the delete: 1,860 costume hires gone, just as before.
options.senior: A log tells you what happened; it stops nothing. And a name in a log is only worth what the name means: with one shared account, every system signs the same name, so the log can't tell them apart. Logs earn their place once each system has its own account, and OWASP asks for refused attempts to be logged too. But noticing comes after preventing, not instead of it.

options.text: Give each system its own account that can reach only the records that system needs.
options.part2: Afonso split theatre_all into three service accounts, boxoffice, costumes and payroll, and gave each a role: a named set of rights that fits one system's work. The box office role may read, change and delete tickets and custom drafts, and nothing else. The printer's job now signs in as boxoffice. We replayed last night in the sim with the slip still in: the database refused the delete, 0 rows, and all 1,860 costume hires stayed. The refusal went into the log, now with the account's name, boxoffice; the job stopped with an error, and Afonso set the job's errors to email him. Then he added attributes, rules about what and when: boxoffice may delete custom drafts only between 02:00 and 03:00, and never tickets, which are marked refunded instead. The grid shows what the job's account may delete: 43,241 bookings as theatre_all, 38,441 with the role alone, 41 with attributes.
options.senior: Authorization decides what each proven identity may do, and least privilege means giving it only what its work needs. One account per system makes every action point to one system, and scoped rights make the database refuse whatever a slip asks for outside them. Roles (RBAC) are easy to read and review; attributes (ABAC) add rules on what, where and when, for the cases roles are too coarse for. The cost is real: more accounts, more passwords, and a regular review of who can do what, or rights pile up again.

sim.title: Replay the 02:00 clean-up against the access grid
sim.lede: You're Afonso, before 02:00 last night. The bookings table holds 38,400 tickets, 41 custom drafts, 1,860 costume hires and 2,940 payroll shifts: 43,241 in all. Choose the accounts (one shared service account, theatre_all, or one per system, where the printer's job signs in as boxoffice), the rights (full rights; roles, where each account may read, change and delete only its own system's kinds; or roles plus attributes, where boxoffice may delete custom drafts only between 02:00 and 03:00, and tickets never), whether last night's slip is in the filter, whether a second person reads the filter first, and the backup (weekly, Sunday 23:00, or nightly, 23:00). The shared account holds every system's rights, so a rule about who is asking can't narrow it. As given data, 64 costume hires were booked after Sunday's 23:00 backup, and 3 after 23:00 last night; a backup put back loses those. Then run the job. The grid shows which account may read (R), change (C) or delete (D) each kind; D* means only between 02:00 and 03:00.
sim.tryThis: Try this: run it as built. The job deletes 1,860 costume hires, the log's name is theatre_all, the weekly backup gives back 1,796 and 64 are lost. Turn on the second reader: 41 drafts deleted, but the grid still lets theatre_all delete payroll's shifts. Try the nightly backup: 1,857 back, 3 lost. Try one account per system with full rights: still 1,860 deleted, now under boxoffice. Then roles: refused, 0 deleted. Then roles plus attributes, and read what the job's account may delete: 41.

explain.oneLine: Nobody broke in. A script the theatre wrote, signed in as an account the theatre made, asked to delete 1,860 costume hires, and the database checked the account's rights and said yes. The slip picked the target; one shared account with full rights let it land. Give each system its own account with only the rights its work needs, and the same slip is refused.

steps.title: Two questions at every door.
steps.text: Authentication proves who is asking: theatre_all gave the right password at 02:00, so the database knew exactly which account it was talking to. Authorization comes second and decides what that proven account may do. The database asks it every time: may this account do this action, such as delete, on these rows? Last night the answer was decided in June, when theatre_all was given full rights over every kind of booking.

steps.title: What happened at 02:00:04, step by step.
steps.text: First the clean-up job signed in as theatre_all. Then it sent its instruction: delete every booking whose kind is 'costume'. Next the database checked the account's rights for a delete on those 1,860 rows, found full rights, and allowed it. Then it deleted them and wrote one line in the audit log: time, DELETE, kind=costume, rows 1,860, allowed. Nothing in that chain was broken. The 44 nights before ran the same chain with 'custom' in the filter, and the same full rights were simply never tested.

steps.title: Why one shared account costs twice.
steps.text: A shared account adds up every system's needs. Box office needs tickets and drafts, costume hire needs costume hires, payroll needs shifts, so theatre_all needs all of them, and any program using it can reach all of them. That is the first cost: a slip anywhere reaches everything. The second is the record. Every system signs the same name, so even a log that names the account can't say which program asked. Last night the only clue was the time.

steps.title: Roles and attributes.
steps.text: Role-based access control (RBAC) gives each account a role, a named set of rights: the box office role may read, change and delete tickets and custom drafts. Attribute-based access control (ABAC) adds rules on facts about the request: who is asking, what kind of row, where from and when. 'boxoffice may delete custom drafts only between 02:00 and 03:00' is an attribute rule. Roles are simple to read and review; attributes cover what roles are too coarse for. Both work best on deny by default: nothing is allowed until a rule allows it.

steps.title: Keeping rights narrow, and keeping them that way.
steps.text: Least privilege means each account gets only what its work needs. Give every system, and ideally every job, its own service account. Scope its rights to the kinds and actions it uses. Log refusals as well as successes, and have errors reach a person. Then review the grid regularly, because rights given for a busy week tend to stay. Backups stay too, as the second line: they don't stop a mistake, they limit what it costs.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn for tonight. On the left, the box office with the printer's clean-up job, costume hire and payroll. Each signs in with its own service account in the middle: boxoffice, costumes, payroll. Each account reaches only its own kinds on the right: boxoffice reaches tickets and custom drafts, costumes reaches costume hires, payroll reaches shifts. A dashed red line from boxoffice to costume hires is marked refused.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for tonight. Each system signs in with its own service account, and each account's role reaches only its own kinds. Last night's slip now asks boxoffice to delete costume hires, and the database refuses: 0 rows deleted, all 1,860 kept, and the refusal logged under boxoffice. With attributes on top, boxoffice may delete only the 41 custom drafts, only between 02:00 and 03:00.

fix.title: The fix: one account per system, each with only the rights it needs
fix.text: Split theatre_all into three service accounts, boxoffice, costumes and payroll, and run the printer's clean-up job as boxoffice (or, better still, as an account of its own). Give each a role that covers only its own kinds of booking: the box office role may read, change and delete tickets and custom drafts; the costume role, costume hires; the payroll role, shifts. Start from deny by default, so anything no rule allows is refused. Add attributes where a role is too wide: boxoffice may delete custom drafts only between 02:00 and 03:00, and never tickets. Log refusals as well as changes, and send the job's errors to a person. Then put the access grid on the calendar: every quarter, read each account's rights against what its system actually does, and remove the rest. In the sim, last night's slip is refused, 0 rows go, and all 1,860 costume hires stay. Keep the backups, and make them nightly: they are the second line, for the slip that stays inside an account's own rows.

limits: Narrow rights stop a slip from crossing systems, not inside one. A box office slip that names the wrong drafts can still delete them; attributes such as 'only drafts older than a day' narrow it further, and backups cover the rest.

More accounts mean more passwords to keep safe and change, and more rules to keep right. Without a regular review, rights given for one busy week tend to stay, and the grid drifts back towards everything.
Rules protect only where they are checked. Here the database checks them; if a system checks rights only inside its own code, anything else holding its account can step around them.

explain.seniorTake: Authentication and authorization are different questions, and most damage from inside a system comes from the second: a real, proven account doing something it should never have been allowed to do. Shared service accounts with full rights are a common shortcut because they save an afternoon, and they quietly turn every slip in every program into a slip against every record. The fix is least privilege applied to programs, not just people: one account per service, ideally per job, scoped to the kinds and actions that service uses, starting from deny by default. Use roles (RBAC) for the broad shape, because people can read and review them, and attributes (ABAC) for the cases roles can't express, such as time windows or 'only rows you created'. Make refusals loud: log them and send them to someone. Then budget for upkeep. Rights drift towards more, never less, unless someone reviews the grid on a calendar. Backups, second readers and logs are all worth having; none of them stops the delete.

realWorld.title: OWASP Top 10:2025, A01 Broken Access Control
realWorld.text: OWASP's description begins: "Access control enforces policy such that users cannot act outside of their intended permissions." It goes on: "Failures typically lead to unauthorized information disclosure, modification or destruction of all data, or performing a business function outside the user's limits." Last night was destruction, by a program acting outside what its work needed.

realWorld.title: OWASP: least privilege, deny by default
realWorld.text: Among the common weaknesses OWASP lists: "Violation of the principle of least privilege, commonly known as deny by default, where access should only be granted for particular capabilities, roles, or users, but is available to anyone." theatre_all was available to every program in the building.

realWorld.title: OWASP: how to prevent it
realWorld.text: Its prevention list includes "Except for public resources, deny by default.", "Model access controls should enforce record ownership rather than allowing users to create, read, update, or delete any record." and "Log access control failures, alert admins when appropriate (e.g., repeated failures)." The fix does all three.

realWorld.title: CIS Control 5: Account Management
realWorld.text: The Center for Internet Security's overview names service accounts directly: "Use processes and tools to assign and manage authorization to credentials for user accounts, including administrator accounts, as well as service accounts, to enterprise assets and software."

realWorld.title: CIS Control 6: Access Control Management
realWorld.text: The overview covers the whole life of a right: "Use processes and tools to create, assign, manage, and revoke access credentials and privileges for user, administrator, and service accounts for enterprise assets and software." Revoke is the step most often forgotten.

realWorld.title: NIST SP 800-162: what ABAC means
realWorld.text: NIST defines it: "ABAC is a logical access control methodology where authorization to perform a set of operations is determined by evaluating attributes associated with the subject, object, requested operations, and, in some cases, environment conditions against policy, rules, or relationships that describe the allowable operations for a given set of attributes." The 02:00 to 03:00 window is an environment condition.

realWorld.title: The same idea for AI: LATENT, Too Much Power
realWorld.text: An AI agent given broad tools is a program with a shared account's reach. LATENT's Too Much Power takes this case's lesson to agents.

asked: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
RBAC or ABAC: when would you choose each?
How do you apply least privilege to services?
interview.answer: Authentication proves who is asking, with a password, a key or a second factor. Authorization decides what that proven identity may do, for each action on each resource, and it is checked on every request, not once at sign-in. For the model, I start with roles, RBAC: each identity gets named sets of rights, such as 'box office' may read, change and delete tickets. Roles are easy to read, audit and review, which matters more than people expect. I add attributes, ABAC, when a rule depends on facts roles can't express: time of day, the row's owner, where the request comes from, how old the record is. NIST describes ABAC as evaluating attributes of the subject, object, operation and environment against policy. Many systems end up with roles for the shape and a few attribute rules for the edges. For services, least privilege means one account per service, ideally per job, never a shared one; scoped to the tables and actions it uses, starting from deny by default; with refusals logged and alerted; and a regular review of who can do what, because rights only ever drift upwards on their own. A story I'd tell: a theatre ran three systems and a nightly clean-up script under one service account with full rights. One typo in the script's filter, 'costume' for 'custom', deleted 1,860 costume hires, and the audit log said 'allowed'. With one account per system and a role each, the same typo is refused and deletes nothing.

terms.def: The theatre in this story. Its box office, costume hire and payroll systems all kept their bookings in one database.
The person at a theatre's backstage entrance who checks passes and knows who may go where. Faustina is the Tollemache's.
A program, or a set of programs, that does one job for the theatre: the box office, costume hire or payroll.
The theatre's ticket-selling system. The ticket printer and its clean-up job belong to it.
The system that rents the theatre's old costumes to schools and touring companies. It held 1,860 bookings for the season.
The system that books staff shifts and pays for them. It held 2,940 shift bookings.
An organised store of records that programs can search and change. All three of the theatre's systems use one.
One list inside a database, with one record per line (row). The theatre's bookings table holds every booking of every kind.
One line of a table: here, one booking.
The label on each booking saying whose it is: ticket, custom (a custom ticket draft), costume or shift.
A name and password that lets someone or something sign in, with a list of what it may do.
An account used by a program, not a person. theatre_all was one, shared by all three systems and the clean-up job.
The theatre's one shared service account, set up in June, with full rights over every booking.
What an account may do: read, change or delete, and on which records. Also called permissions.
Rights to read, change and delete everything. theatre_all had them over all 43,241 bookings.
A gift ticket printed with a guest's name. Drafts that are never printed are deleted each night by the clean-up job.
A small program that runs a list of instructions, often on a timer.
The script that runs at 02:00 every night, since 1 September, to delete the ticket printer's unused custom drafts.
The part of an instruction that picks which rows it acts on, such as WHERE kind = 'custom'.
The instruction that removes rows from a table. Without a backup, they are gone.
A database's own diary of changes: when, what action, which kind, how many rows, and whether it was allowed. The theatre's didn't record the account.
A safety copy of the database, so it can be put back after a loss. The theatre's was weekly, on Sunday at 23:00.
Proving who someone or something is, for example with a password. Taught in Who Are You.
Deciding what a proven identity may do: which actions, on which records. Checked on every request.
A named set of rights that fits one job, such as 'box office: read, change and delete tickets and custom drafts'.
Short for role-based access control: each account gets one or more roles, and its rights are whatever those roles allow.
A fact about a request: who is asking, what kind of record, where from, and when.
Short for attribute-based access control: rights decided by rules on attributes, such as 'boxoffice may delete custom drafts only between 02:00 and 03:00'.
Giving every account only the rights its work needs, and nothing more, like a dresser's pass that opens wardrobe and nothing else.
Nothing is allowed until a rule allows it, so a missing rule means a refusal, not an open door.
Rights limited to particular kinds of record and particular actions, instead of everything.
A regular check of who, or which program, can do what, against what each one needs, removing the rest.
A table of accounts against kinds of record, showing which may read, change or delete each. The sim draws one.
A person who reads a change, here a script's filter, before it runs, to catch mistakes. Quirino's suggestion.
A person who collects or delivers goods. The stage door lets them in for costume collections listed at 06:00.
The Open Worldwide Application Security Project, a non-profit that publishes free guidance on web application security.
OWASP's list of the ten most important web application security risks. In the 2025 edition, A01 is Broken Access Control.
Any failure of authorization: a user or program able to read, change or delete what it shouldn't.
The Center for Internet Security's prioritised list of security safeguards. Control 5 covers accounts; Control 6, access control.
The US National Institute of Standards and Technology. Its SP 800-162 defines ABAC.
An AI program that can take actions with tools, such as sending email or changing records, not just answer.
An international standard for managing information security. Its Annex A lists controls, including several on access.
An audit of a company's security controls against the Trust Services Criteria, set by the American Institute of CPAs. Its CC6 criteria cover logical access.
The list of controls at the back of ISO/IEC 27001, such as A.5.15 access control and A.5.18 access rights.

atWork: Look for service accounts shared by more than one program, and for any program whose account has full rights it never uses. It is a common pattern: one database login set up for the first app 'to save time', then reused by a report, a nightly script and a second app, until one typo in any of them can reach everything. For each service account, ask four questions. Which programs sign in with it? Which tables and actions does each of them actually use? What could it delete right now? And if it did, would your log say which program asked? Then draw your own access grid and narrow it: one account per service, ideally per job, scoped to what it uses, starting from deny by default, with refusals logged and sent to a person. Put a review of the grid on the calendar. In Build Night N5 you build roles into the uptime monitor: decide what each role may do, and write the test that proves a refused action is refused. Standards: if your company is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001:2022, this is Annex A 5.15 (access control), 5.18 (access rights, including regular review) and 8.2 (privileged access rights); if it is pursuing SOC 2, it is CC6.1 (logical access security) and CC6.3 (access based on roles, with least privilege). A shared full-rights service account is a finding an auditor is likely to raise under each, so build per-service accounts and a review record from the first draft rather than at audit time.

recall.prompt: Your company runs three services, orders, invoices and a nightly reporting job, and all three sign in to the database with the same login, which has administrator rights. Last night a bug in the reporting job emptied the invoices table. The audit log shows that login and 'allowed'. A colleague wants every job's code read by a second engineer before it ships. What went wrong, and what would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: One shared login with full rights let a reporting job reach invoices it never needed
Give each service its own account with only the rights its work needs: least privilege, read only for the report
Then the database refuses the next bug outside that scope, whatever a reviewer misses

recall.model: The bug was the trigger, but the damage came from the login. One shared login with full rights let a reporting job reach invoices it never needed, and the database said yes. Give each service its own account, scoped by least privilege: the reporting job gets read only, on the tables it reports on, and nothing else. Then the next bug that tries to empty invoices is refused by the database, whoever wrote it and whatever the reviewer missed. A second reader is a fine habit, but it can't stop the bug a reader misses. With separate accounts the audit log also says which service asked, and refusals can be logged and sent to someone.

options: What may you do, now that we know who you are?
Has this booking been backed up?
recall.why: Authentication proves who is asking; authorization decides what that proven identity may do. theatre_all passed the first at 02:00 and was given everything by the second.

recall.prompt: Which rule is attribute-based (ABAC), not just role-based (RBAC)?
options: The box office role may delete custom drafts
The payroll account may read shifts
boxoffice may delete custom drafts only between 02:00 and 03:00
Every system signs in under a different name
recall.why: A time window is a fact about the request, an environment condition in NIST's words, which a role alone can't express. The first two are plain role rights; the last is about accounts, not rules.

recall.prompt: In the sim, with one account per system and roles, the printer's job runs last night's slip. What happens?
options: It deletes 1,860 costume hires, but the log names boxoffice
The database refuses the delete: 0 rows go, and all 1,860 costume hires stay
It deletes the 41 custom drafts instead
It deletes every booking in the table
recall.why: The box office role covers tickets and custom drafts only, so a delete on costume hires is refused. With one account per system but full rights, the first answer is what happens: a better name in the log, the same loss.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 5 months later. Three service accounts now, boxoffice, costumes and payroll, each with its own role, and the clean-up job has been refused twice for slips Afonso caught in its error emails. In December, for the pantomime rush, Afonso gave the costumes account the box office role too, so Bronislava's desk could sell tickets while the queue ran out of the door. The rush ended in January. Nobody touched the role. In March the costume system's yearly tidy, which deletes every booking made before 1 January and has no kind in its filter, ran under costumes. It deleted 212 ticket bookings for the spring gala, all sold in December. The audit log names costumes. Every line says allowed.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why could the costume tidy delete tickets, and what should the theatre do so an extra right like that doesn't linger?

keyIdeas.idea: A temporary extra role was never taken away, so the costumes account had more than its work needs
Review who can do what regularly, against what each system needs
Give temporary rights an end date, so they expire on their own

coldCase.model: The tidy did what its filter said, and the costumes account still had the box office role from December, so the database allowed it. A temporary right was never taken away, and nothing checked. Give every temporary right an end date so it expires by itself, here at the end of January. Then run an access review every quarter: for each account, list what it may do against what its system needs, and remove the rest. The access grid would have shown costumes able to delete tickets in a minute. And a tidy with no kind in its filter is safe only while its account is narrow, so add the kind too. Least privilege isn't set once; it drifts unless someone looks.
